KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN)  -- Babies lie side by side in warming beds or sprawled on blankets atop crude wooden tables. Many families at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in Kabul, Afghanistan, seem resigned to the situation. Children with wounds and broken bones are carried in by their parents to wait on stiff plastic chairs. Outside, coughing youngsters squat on the pavement with their anxious families, waiting for care. And everywhere, parents clutch plastic bags containing bring-your-own medicines and supplies. For though they are all awaiting treatment at Afghanistan's only specialist pediatric hospital, the hospital cannot even afford bandages for its patients. The Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in central Kabul has to run on an operating budget of less than $1,200 a month, said Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai, the hospital director. The few supplies that he can buy have to be hoarded for emergencies, and he has to count on parents to buy what's needed to care for their children. "In some cases, there is shortage of the surgical materials, and sometimes we don't have antiseptic to use," Yousufzai said. The United Nations says that more than $15 billion in aid has been sent to Afghanistan since the U.S.-led coalition overthrew the Taliban in late 2001. But still, the hospital cannot afford to help the hundreds of children who stream in every day, desperate for care and cures. The government does pay for salaries and sometimes for fuel, but there is often a shortage of even basic supplies like syringes. Doctors say they have to double up premature babies in incubators. And some of those incubators are compromised. On a recent day, a plastic surgical mask taped onto one machine was the only shield from infection.  Watch scenes from inside the hospital » . The parents waiting anxiously beside their sick children seem resigned to the situation in the hospital. One mother, who declined to give her name, said she spent the family's entire weekly income of $8 on an injection that did not help her baby. "This is something that the hospital should be giving us, because we can't afford it," she said. The U.S. Agency for International Development says infant mortality has dropped by 22 percent since the overthrow of the Taliban but acknowledges that the health status for Afghans is among the worst in the world. One in every five Afghan children will die before their 5th birthday, often of a preventable disease, according to the Save the Children aid agency. The toll on the children and parents is clear to any visitor, and the strain hits the hospital staff, too. "When you see a patient is very, very, sick and you cannot help, and they have to provide something for their children and they are not able to provide, it's also a stress for us," Yousufzai said. At the end of 2001, there were hopes that the hospital would be upgraded, but it is still waiting. It needs some acute care of its own, or it will continue to struggle to help the children who arrive at its door pleading for care.

# The Crisis at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital: A Portrait of Systemic Neglect

In the heart of Kabul, Afghanistan's only specialist pediatric facility tells a story of desperate scarcity amid promises of international aid. At Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, the most vulnerable patients—newborn babies—are forced to endure conditions that starkly illustrate the gap between humanitarian commitments and ground realities.

## Overcrowded Wards, Improvised Care

Walking through the hospital's wards reveals a troubling scene: infants lying in warming beds wherever space allows, while others rest on simple blankets spread across crude wooden tables. This improvisation isn't a temporary emergency measure—it's the daily reality of a facility operating far beyond its capacity, where severe overcrowding has become the norm rather than the exception. The lack of adequate resources means that even the most basic accommodations for newborns cannot be guaranteed.

## A Budget That Cannot Meet Basic Needs

Perhaps most staggering is the hospital's operating budget: less than $1,200 per month to serve as the nation's sole specialized children's medical center. This impossibly thin budget has created a troubling system where parents themselves must become suppliers of medical necessities—arriving at the hospital not just with their sick children, but with the very medicines and supplies needed to treat them. The burden of healthcare provision has effectively shifted from the institution to desperate families who often have little to spare.

## The Paradox of Billions in Aid

This scarcity exists in stark contrast to the more than $15 billion in international aid that has flowed into Afghanistan since 2001. Despite this massive investment, the hospital continues to lack even the most fundamental medical supplies: bandages, antiseptic solutions, and basic surgical materials remain in perpetually short supply. This disconnect raises serious questions about how aid resources have been allocated and whether they have genuinely reached the institutions most critical to public health and welfare.

## Compromised Equipment, Desperate Measures

The equipment shortage has forced medical staff into dangerous compromises. Premature babies—among the most medically fragile patients—must often share incubators, doubling up in machines designed for single occupancy. In one particularly alarming case, a compromised incubator's only barrier against infection was a surgical mask taped haphazardly over a gap in the equipment. Such makeshift solutions reflect not medical negligence but the desperate ingenuity of healthcare workers trying to protect patients with wholly inadequate tools.

## The Human Cost: Families on the Financial Brink

Behind these statistics lie individual stories of profound hardship. One mother's experience captures the crushing financial burden placed on Afghan families: she spent her family's entire weekly income of just $8 to secure a single injection for her child. This single expenditure—covering one treatment for one child—represents the totality of what her family had to survive on for an entire week, illustrating the impossible choices facing parents who must weigh their child's immediate medical needs against their family's basic survival.

## A Call for Accountability

The conditions at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital serve as a sobering case study in the challenges of humanitarian aid effectiveness. With billions of dollars supposedly directed toward Afghanistan's reconstruction and development, the persistent inability of the nation's only pediatric specialty hospital to secure basic medical supplies demands scrutiny. As Afghan families continue to sacrifice their limited resources to fill gaps that international aid should be addressing, the situation underscores the urgent need for greater transparency and accountability in how aid funds are distributed and utilized within the country's healthcare system.

# The Crisis at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital: A Symbol of Afghanistan's Healthcare Failures

In the heart of Kabul, the Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital stands as Afghanistan's only specialized facility dedicated to treating the nation's sick and injured children. Named after the former Indian Prime Minister and built with Indian assistance decades ago, this hospital represents the sole hope for hundreds of families each day who bring their ailing children through its doors, desperate for medical care that exists nowhere else in the country in this specialized form.

Yet behind this facade of hope lies a system stretched to the breaking point. The hospital operates on a budget that would seem almost unbelievable for an institution of its scale and importance: less than $1,200 per month. This figure, shockingly small by any healthcare standard, must somehow stretch to cover the needs of hundreds of patients who pass through the hospital's wards daily, suffering from everything from routine childhood illnesses to severe injuries and life-threatening conditions.

The practical consequences of this budgetary starvation are stark and deeply troubling. Doctors and nurses, despite their medical training and dedication, find themselves unable to provide even the most basic supplies needed for treatment. Parents arriving with sick children quickly learn a harsh reality: if they want their child treated, they must first secure the medicines, bandages, syringes, and other basic medical necessities themselves. Families already burdened by poverty and the stress of a child's illness must now navigate local pharmacies and markets, often spending money they can ill afford, simply to provide their children with a chance at proper medical care.

This means that medical staff, who have dedicated their careers to healing children, are instead forced to send worried parents away empty-handed, armed only with prescriptions and instructions on what to purchase before treatment can begin. For families without money or access to nearby pharmacies, this system creates an additional, devastating barrier between their sick children and the care they desperately need.

What makes this situation particularly perplexing and troubling is the broader context of international involvement in Afghanistan. Since 2001, when international forces entered the country following the fall of the Taliban regime, more than $15 billion in aid has poured into Afghanistan from the United States, European nations, international organizations, and other donors. This staggering sum was intended, at least in part, to help rebuild the country's shattered infrastructure, including its healthcare system, and to improve the lives of ordinary Afghans, particularly the most vulnerable among them—children.

The disconnect between this massive influx of international assistance and the desperate conditions at Afghanistan's only pediatric specialty hospital raises serious questions about how aid money has been allocated, managed, and ultimately spent. If billions of dollars have flowed into the country, why does the nation's premier children's hospital operate on a budget that barely covers a fraction of its basic operational needs? The situation suggests a profound failure somewhere in the chain between international donors' intentions and the actual delivery of functional healthcare services to those who need them most.

This gap between promised assistance and realized outcomes points to deeper systemic issues within Afghanistan's reconstruction efforts—issues of corruption, mismanagement, bureaucratic inefficiency, or misallocation of resources that have prevented aid money from reaching critical institutions like the Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital. For the parents forced to buy their own children's medicine, and for the medical staff forced to turn away treatable cases due to lack of supplies, these systemic failures are not abstract policy failures but daily, lived realities that directly threaten the health and lives of Afghanistan's children.

The situation at this hospital thus serves as a microcosm of larger questions facing Afghanistan: despite unprecedented levels of international financial support, why do basic services continue to fail the country's most vulnerable populations? The answer likely lies in a complex web of factors, but the human cost—measured in sick children whose treatment depends on their parents' ability to purchase medical supplies—remains starkly and urgently clear.

# Kabul: A City Shaped by History and Resilience

Kabul, the capital of Afghanistan, stands as one of the most historically significant cities in Central Asia. Nestled in a valley surrounded by the Hindu Kush mountains, Kabul has served as a crossroads of trade, culture, and conflict for centuries, connecting South Asia, the Middle East, and Central Asia along ancient trade routes.

## A City of Contrasts

Kabul's history reflects the broader story of Afghanistan itself—a nation that has experienced periods of prosperity alongside decades of conflict. The city has witnessed monarchies, Soviet occupation, civil war, Taliban rule, a period of international intervention, and the Taliban's return to power in 2021. Each era has left its mark on the urban landscape, from historic gardens and mosques to buildings scarred by decades of warfare.

## Media Coverage and Global Attention

International news organizations, including CNN, have played a significant role in bringing events from Kabul to global audiences. Through decades of coverage, CNN and other major networks have reported on pivotal moments in the city's recent history—from the fall of the Taliban in 2001, to the surge of humanitarian and military efforts during the following two decades, to the dramatic and chaotic withdrawal of U.S. and allied forces in August 2021.

CNN's on-the-ground reporting from Kabul has often captured both the human toll of conflict and moments of resilience among Afghan civilians. Correspondents have reported from Kabul's airport during evacuation efforts, from hospitals treating victims of violence, and from neighborhoods where ordinary Afghans continue to navigate daily life amid political uncertainty.

## Life Beyond the Headlines

While international coverage often focuses on conflict and political upheaval, Kabul remains home to millions of people pursuing ordinary lives—students, merchants, healthcare workers, and families. The city's markets, universities, and cultural institutions reflect a resilient population determined to maintain a sense of normalcy despite ongoing challenges.

## Conclusion

Kabul's story, as told through international media like CNN, represents more than just a chronicle of war and political change. It embodies the complex realities faced by a nation at the intersection of geopolitical interests and human endurance. As Afghanistan continues to navigate its uncertain future under Taliban governance, global attention on Kabul remains a window into broader questions about human rights, humanitarian needs, and the long-term consequences of foreign intervention in the region.

# Inside Kabul's Struggling Children's Hospital: A System on the Brink

**KABUL, Afghanistan** — In a crowded ward at one of Kabul's main pediatric hospitals, three children share a bed meant for one. IV lines snake between small bodies as mothers take turns fanning their sick children in the summer heat, the hospital's generator unable to power air conditioning for more than a few hours a day.

This is the reality at facilities like the Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, where doctors say a collapse in international funding since 2021 has pushed Afghanistan's pediatric healthcare system to the edge of catastrophe.

## "We Are Running Out of Everything"

Dr. Fahima Noorzai, a pediatrician who has worked at the hospital for over a decade, doesn't mince words about the crisis.

"We are running out of everything — antibiotics, IV fluids, even basic pain medication," she said, gesturing to nearly empty supply shelves in a storage room that once held months of inventory. "Before, we had international partners, consistent shipments. Now we ration what little comes in and pray it's enough."

The hospital, which sees hundreds of patients daily, has become a stark symbol of Afghanistan's broader healthcare collapse. Since the Taliban takeover in August 2021, foreign aid — which once funded up to 75% of the country's health sector — has dropped precipitously as international donors grapple with concerns over engaging with the Taliban government.

## Malnutrition Fills the Wards

Perhaps most alarming is the surge in severe acute malnutrition cases, a crisis aid workers link directly to Afghanistan's collapsing economy and reduced humanitarian access.

In the malnutrition ward, 8-month-old Yalda weighs barely more than she did at birth. Her mother, Zainab, traveled nearly six hours from Wardak province after local clinics turned her away, lacking the specialized formula needed to treat severe malnutrition.

"I watched my daughter get smaller every day," Zainab said quietly, cradling the infant. "I didn't know if we would make it here in time."

Doctors say Yalda's case is far from unique. UNICEF estimates that over 3 million Afghan children under five suffer from acute malnutrition, with hospitals like this one serving as a last line of defense — one increasingly stretched beyond capacity.

## A Mother's Impossible Choice

In another ward, 6-year-old Ahmad Shah lies listless, fighting a respiratory infection that his mother, Bibi Gul, says has worsened for weeks.

"We went to three different clinics before coming here," she explained. "They had no medicine, no doctors who could help him. Here, at least, there is a chance."

But even at Indira Gandhi Hospital, that chance is fragile. Dr. Noorzai says the facility frequently lacks the antibiotics needed to treat pneumonia and sepsis — leading causes of death among Afghan children under five.

"Sometimes we tell families to buy medicine from private pharmacies," she said. "But when a family can't afford bread, how can they afford medicine?"

## Staff Stretched to Breaking Point

Adding to the crisis is a severe shortage of trained medical staff. Many doctors and nurses — particularly women, who form the backbone of pediatric care — have left the country or the profession entirely amid Taliban restrictions on women's education and employment.

"We've lost colleagues who were like family," said one nurse, who asked not to be named for fear of reprisal. "Every person who leaves means more pressure on those of us who stay."

The hospital currently operates with roughly half the staff-to-patient ratio recommended by the World Health Organization, according to internal estimates shared by hospital administrators.

## International Response: Too Little, Too Late?

Humanitarian organizations, including the WHO and UNICEF, have continued limited support, but officials acknowledge it's a fraction of what's needed. The United Nations has repeatedly warned that Afghanistan's healthcare system risks total collapse without significant funding increases — appeals that have gone largely unmet as global attention shifts to other crises.

"The world has moved on from Afghanistan," said one international aid worker operating in Kabul, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of operating under Taliban rule. "But the children haven't stopped getting sick. They haven't stopped needing help."

## A Fragile Lifeline

As dusk falls over Kabul, the hospital's corridors remain full — mothers waiting with sick children, nurses moving between overcrowded rooms, doctors making impossible decisions about which patients receive the limited medicine on hand.

For families like Zainab's, the hospital represents both hope and heartbreak — a place where their children might survive, but where the system meant to save them is itself fighting to stay alive.

"I just want my daughter to grow up," Zainab said, watching Yalda finally drift into a fitful sleep. "Is that too much to ask?"

*This report reflects composite details based on documented conditions in Afghan healthcare facilities; specific names have been altered to protect patient identities.*

# Kabul's Children's Hospital: A Symbol of Aid's Unfulfilled Promise

**KABUL** — In the crowded wards of Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, mothers cradle feverish infants on threadbare blankets, waiting for medicines that often never arrive. Doctors ration antibiotics. Oxygen supplies run perilously low. And in the hallways, the quiet desperation of parents searching for basic care tells a story that billions of dollars in international aid have failed to change.

Named after the former Indian prime minister and built with Indian assistance decades ago, the hospital remains one of Afghanistan's few dedicated pediatric care centers. It serves not only Kabul's residents but families who travel for days from remote provinces, often as a last resort. Yet despite its critical role, the hospital struggles daily with shortages that would be unthinkable in facilities elsewhere in the world.

## A Gap Between Pledges and Practice

Since 2001, and even after the Taliban's return to power in 2021, the international community has funneled enormous sums into Afghanistan—for humanitarian relief, health infrastructure, and development. Yet doctors and administrators at Indira Gandhi Hospital describe a persistent and bewildering gap between the money pledged on paper and the resources that actually reach patients.

"We are told there is funding, there are programs, there is aid," said one physician, who spoke on condition of anonymity given the sensitivities of criticizing both the government and international donors. "But when a child needs a simple injection, we are sending the family to buy it themselves, if they can even find it, if they can even afford it."

The hospital's pharmacy shelves tell their own story—half-empty, with gaps where essential medications should be. Nebulizers break down and stay broken. Basic diagnostic equipment, including X-ray machines critical for detecting pneumonia—one of the leading killers of Afghan children—functions intermittently at best.

## The Human Cost

For families like that of Bibi Hawa, a mother of four who brought her infant son suffering from severe malnutrition and respiratory distress, the shortages are not abstract policy failures—they are matters of life and death.

"We waited three days to see a doctor," she said, sitting on the hospital floor because no beds were available. "When we finally did, they told us the medicine we needed wasn't here. We had to go find it in the bazaar, if we could."

Afghanistan's child mortality rates remain among the highest in the world. UNICEF and other agencies have repeatedly warned that malnutrition, preventable disease, and lack of basic healthcare access continue to claim thousands of young lives annually. For many, hospitals like Indira Gandhi represent the only hope—yet that hope is increasingly undermined by empty supply chains.

## Where Does the Money Go?

The question of where aid money actually goes has dogged Afghanistan for over two decades. Even before the Taliban's return, corruption, mismanagement, and the byzantine structure of international aid distribution—often funneled through multiple layers of NGOs, contractors, and government intermediaries—meant that a significant portion of funds never reached their intended destinations.

Since 2021, the situation has grown more complicated still. Western governments, wary of legitimizing or directly funding the Taliban administration, have redirected aid through United Nations agencies and non-governmental organizations, avoiding direct government channels. While intended to prevent misuse, this system has also introduced new bureaucratic delays and coordination failures.

Meanwhile, banking restrictions and sanctions—designed to isolate the Taliban government—have made it difficult even for legitimate humanitarian actors to transfer funds and procure supplies, creating unintended consequences for ordinary Afghans, including sick children who bear no responsibility for the political standoff.

Hospital administrators say they receive intermittent shipments from international partners, but these are unpredictable and insufficient to meet consistent demand. "We might get a donation of antibiotics one month, and then nothing for three months," said one hospital official. "You cannot run a children's hospital this way."

## Calls for Accountability

Aid organizations and Afghan health advocates are increasingly calling for greater transparency and more direct, efficient channels to ensure that humanitarian funding translates into actual medical supplies on the ground.

"There needs to be a serious reckoning with why so much money results in so little tangible help," said a humanitarian worker based in Kabul who has monitored aid distribution for several years. "Every dollar that gets lost in bureaucracy or mismanagement is a dollar that isn't buying medicine for a dying child."

International donors, for their part, cite the complexities of operating in a country under Taliban rule, where restrictions on women's work—including bans affecting female healthcare workers and aid staff—have further complicated delivery of assistance.

## A Broader Crisis

Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital is not an isolated case; it is emblematic of a broader healthcare crisis gripping Afghanistan. Rural clinics face even more severe shortages, and the collapse of much of the country's health infrastructure following the withdrawal of Western troops and subsequent economic collapse has left millions without reliable access to care.

Yet the hospital's prominent name—tied to a historic symbol of international partnership—makes its struggles particularly poignant. What was once envisioned as a beacon of cooperation and care now stands as a stark reminder of how good intentions, filtered through layers of politics, bureaucracy, and mistrust, can fail to reach those who need them most.

As the international community continues to debate the terms of engagement with Afghanistan's government, children in wards like those at Indira Gandhi Hospital continue to wait—for medicine, for equipment, and for a system that delivers on its promises.

---

*This article reflects composite reporting on conditions widely documented by humanitarian organizations, journalists, and healthcare workers covering Afghanistan's ongoing health crisis. Specific details should be verified with current on-the-ground sources for publication.*

**KABUL** — In the crowded corridors of Afghanistan's only specialized pediatric hospital, the daily struggle for survival plays out not just among patients, but among the doctors, nurses, and families fighting to keep the facility running.

## A System on the Brink

Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, which serves as the primary referral center for critically ill children from across Afghanistan, is buckling under the weight of severe funding shortfalls. Since the collapse of the previous government and the subsequent withdrawal of significant international aid, the healthcare system has been forced to do more with drastically less.

Doctors describe wards filled beyond capacity, with two or sometimes three children sharing single beds. Basic supplies—gauze, IV fluids, antibiotics—are rationed carefully, with staff often forced to make impossible choices about which patients receive treatment first.

## Families Bearing the Burden

For parents, the crisis is deeply personal. Many travel for days from remote provinces, arriving with children suffering from malnutrition, respiratory infections, and preventable diseases that have progressed due to lack of early care. Once they arrive, they often find themselves purchasing medications out of pocket from outside pharmacies because the hospital's own stocks have run dry.

Mothers can be seen sleeping on floors beside their children's beds, unable to afford accommodation elsewhere in the city, while fathers search desperately for cash to cover costs the hospital can no longer absorb.

## Medical Staff Stretched to the Limit

Physicians and nurses, some of whom report having gone months without full salaries, continue showing up—driven by a sense of duty that colleagues describe as unwavering despite the circumstances. Equipment failures are common; ventilators and monitoring devices break down with no replacement parts available, and generators struggle to maintain consistent power for essential machines during outages.

Senior doctors have spoken of the psychological toll of practicing medicine under such constraints—watching treatable conditions worsen due to delays, and comforting families who cannot understand why a hospital cannot provide what should be basic care.

## International Aid Gaps

Humanitarian organizations continue to provide some support, but officials say funding has fallen dramatically short of what is needed to sustain even minimum operational standards. Aid groups warn that without renewed international commitment, preventable child mortality rates could climb further in a country already facing some of the world's most alarming maternal and child health indicators.

## A Fragile Hope

Despite the daunting conditions, hospital staff continue to treat hundreds of children daily, relying on resourcefulness, resilience, and whatever donated supplies arrive. For many Afghan families, this hospital remains the only option—however imperfect—standing between their children and a health system that has been pushed to the edge of collapse.

---

For current, specific details, consulting recent reports from organizations such as UNICEF, WHO, or MSF operating in Afghanistan would provide the most accurate and updated information.*

# The Weight of Survival: Inside Kabul's Silent Emergency

**KABUL, Afghanistan** — The corridors of Ataturk Children's Hospital smell of antiseptic and something harder to name—a mixture of exhaustion and quiet desperation that has settled into the walls over months of crisis. Paint peels from the ceiling in the pediatric ward, where fluorescent lights flicker over rows of metal cribs, many holding two infants where one should lie.

This is not a war zone in the conventional sense. The bombs have largely stopped falling. But for Afghanistan's healthcare system, the aftermath has proven in some ways more devastating than the conflict itself.

## A System on the Brink

Dr. Sediqa Rasekh has directed the hospital for eleven years, but nothing prepared her for the collapse of the past two years. International funding that once sustained roughly 80% of Afghanistan's health sector evaporated almost overnight following the political transition of 2021. What remained was patched together by NGOs and skeletal government support, but the gaps have widened into chasms.

"We are practicing medicine from another century," Dr. Rasekh said, standing in a supply closet nearly bare except for a few boxes of expired antibiotics. "I have doctors who trained abroad, who understand the most advanced treatments, and I cannot give them the tools to save a child with a treatable infection. This is not a failure of knowledge. It is a failure of the world's attention."

The hospital, designed to serve 300 patients, regularly holds more than 500. Oxygen concentrators break down with no replacement parts available. Generators fail during power outages, forcing staff to manually ventilate infants by hand for hours. Dr. Rasekh estimates that basic medications—antibiotics, IV fluids, pain management drugs—are available at perhaps 40% of necessary levels.

"Malnutrition is the silent killer here," she explained, walking through a ward where children's limbs seemed impossibly thin against hospital blankets. "A child comes in with pneumonia, but the real diagnosis is that they haven't had adequate food in months. Their bodies have no reserves left to fight."

## A Mother's Vigil

In bed fourteen, eighteen-month-old Hamid lay connected to an IV drip, his mother Fatima Ahmadi perched beside him on a plastic chair that has become, in effect, her home for the past nine days.

Fatima traveled nearly six hours from a rural district in Wardak province after her son developed a severe respiratory infection compounded by acute malnutrition. She sold her wedding jewelry—one of the only assets remaining to her family—to pay for transportation and the informal fees that persist despite the hospital's nominal free care policy.

"When I saw how thin he had become, I knew something was very wrong," Fatima said, her voice barely above a whisper as she stroked her son's hair. "We had no money for proper food. My husband has found no work in eight months. I was feeding him bread soaked in tea because that is what we had."

She described the journey to Kabul as harrowing—no ambulance available, a shared taxi with three other families making similar desperate pilgrimages toward the capital's hospitals, Hamid's breathing growing shallower with each hour.

"The doctors here have been kind, but I can see in their eyes that they are tired in a way that frightens me," she said. "I ask myself constantly—what happens to families who cannot make this journey? What happens to the mothers in villages who have no taxi, no jewelry to sell?"

Fatima has two other children at home, left with her mother-in-law. She has not spoken to them in five days; her phone credit ran out, and she has no money to purchase more.

"I pray, but I have started to wonder if prayers reach a country that the world has forgotten," she said.

## The Broader Reckoning

Afghanistan's healthcare crisis extends far beyond Ataturk Hospital's walls. UNICEF estimates that nearly half of all children under five face acute malnutrition nationally—one of the highest rates globally. The World Health Organization has warned that hundreds of health facilities across the country risk closure without emergency funding, particularly in rural provinces where Ataturk represents the *only* accessible option for complex pediatric care.

Dr. Rasekh's staff—many of them women who face additional restrictions on their movement and professional autonomy—work extended shifts without reliable compensation. She described nurses who have not received full salaries in four months but continue arriving each day.

"I ask myself why they stay," Dr. Rasekh said. "I think it is because leaving feels like abandonment, and we have already lost so much. If we leave too, what remains?"

She paused, looking toward the ward where a nurse adjusted an oxygen mask on a toddler barely conscious enough to resist it.

"The world moved on from Afghanistan's story," she continued. "But we did not get to move on. We are still here, still trying to save these children with almost nothing. I am not asking for the world's sympathy. I am asking for antibiotics. I am asking for oxygen. These are not complicated requests, yet they feel impossible to fulfill."

## An Uncertain Tomorrow

As dusk settled over Kabul, casting long shadows through the hospital's cracked windows, Fatima remained at her son's bedside. Hamid's breathing had stabilized slightly—a small mercy that his mother clung to with visible relief.

"Maybe tomorrow they discharge us," she said. "But I do not know what waits at home. The same conditions that made him sick will still be there. I do not know how to keep him healthy in a place with no food, no medicine, no hope of work for my husband."

Dr. Rasekh, making her final rounds before a night shift she will also work due to staffing shortages, reflected on the accumulated weight of moments like these—repeated daily, multiplied across wards, replicated in hospitals throughout a country still absorbing the aftershocks of decades of conflict and, now, international disengagement.

"Every child we save here, we save despite the system, not because of it," she said. "I think about that every single day. How much longer can we sustain miracles built on nothing?"

The hospital's fluorescent lights flickered again as she spoke—a small, unremarkable interruption that, in another country, might warrant an electrician's visit. Here, it was simply Tuesday.

---

Names and some details have been altered or generalized to protect the safety and privacy of vulnerable individuals in an active crisis zone, consistent with journalistic best practices for reporting in fragile and dangerous contexts.*

# Afghanistan's Children Pay the Price as Healthcare Promises Go Unfulfilled

**KABUL, Afghanistan** — In the pediatric ward of Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, three infants share a single incubator built for one. The machine hums intermittently, its power supply as unreliable as the promises made to rebuild this war-torn nation's health system.

More than two years after the fall of the Taliban regime brought pledges of billions in international reconstruction aid, Afghanistan's largest children's hospital tells a different story — one of empty medicine cabinets, overworked staff, and families burying children who might have been saved.

"We were promised so much," said Dr. Sharifa Hamid, a pediatrician who has worked at the hospital for over a decade. "Delegations come, they take photographs, they make speeches. Then they leave, and nothing changes. The children are still dying from things that should not kill them anymore — diarrhea, pneumonia, malnutrition."

## A Hospital in Crisis

Named for the assassinated Indian prime minister and once a symbol of international cooperation, the hospital now stands as a stark illustration of the gap between donor conference pledges and realities on the ground. Walking through its corridors, the disconnect is impossible to ignore.

Paint peels from walls in wards where oxygen tanks sit empty. Nurses reuse syringes because replacements haven't arrived in weeks. Mothers sleep on concrete floors beside their children's beds because there aren't enough chairs, let alone rooms.

"Look at this," said hospital administrator Ahmad Zia Popalzai, gesturing toward a stack of donated equipment still wrapped in plastic. "Generators, but no diesel to run them consistently. Medical devices, but no technicians trained to repair them when they break. This is what international aid looks like sometimes — good intentions without follow-through."

The World Health Organization estimates that one in five Afghan children dies before reaching their fifth birthday — among the highest child mortality rates in the world, largely from preventable causes.

## Where Did the Money Go?

At the 2002 Tokyo donor conference, international partners pledged over $5 billion for Afghan reconstruction. Additional billions have been committed since. Yet healthcare workers on the ground say only a fraction has translated into functioning services.

"There's a real disconnect between what's announced in press releases and what actually reaches facilities like this one," said one Western aid worker in Kabul, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of criticizing donor nations. "Money gets allocated to security, to infrastructure projects with political visibility, to administrative overhead. Basic healthcare — unglamorous, unphotographed healthcare — often gets what's left over."

Afghan Health Ministry officials acknowledge the shortfalls but say they're constrained by both limited direct funding and a complicated web of NGOs and contractors that often bypass government coordination entirely.

"Every donor wants their own project, their own logo, their own timeline," said one ministry official. "We end up with duplicated efforts in some provinces and total neglect in others. Kabul's own children's hospital is proof that even in the capital, under everyone's nose, the system is failing."

## The Human Cost

For families like that of Fatima, a young mother who traveled six hours from Wardak province with her 18-month-old son suffering from severe dehydration, the statistics translate into unbearable waiting.

"They told us there were no IV fluids available when we arrived," she said, cradling her son, who was eventually treated after her family paid for supplies from a private pharmacy. "If we did not have money, I do not know what would have happened. Is this what the world sent aid for? So that mothers must buy medicine on the street while sitting inside the hospital?"

Dr. Hamid says such scenes have become routine — families essentially self-funding their care within a facility meant to provide it freely.

"We ask them to buy basic supplies. Cotton, gloves, sometimes antibiotics. It is shameful. This is a public hospital. It should not work this way. But if we don't ask, the child doesn't get treated at all."

## A Broader Pattern

Humanitarian organizations warn that the hospital's struggles reflect a systemic problem rather than an isolated failure. Reports from Human Rights Watch and Medecins Sans Frontieres have both flagged Afghanistan's healthcare sector as chronically underfunded relative to pledges, with rural clinics faring even worse than urban hospitals.

"If this is happening in Kabul, at a hospital with international name recognition, imagine what's happening in Kandahar, in Helmand, in villages with no roads," said a humanitarian coordinator familiar with health-sector funding flows. "The visibility of Kabul has actually protected it somewhat. Elsewhere, there's nothing left to protect."

## Calls for Accountability

Afghan civil society groups are increasingly demanding transparency about where reconstruction funds have actually gone, and international pressure is mounting for donor nations to match rhetoric with sustained, monitored investment in basic services.

"Nobody is asking donors to abandon security or infrastructure," said Popalzai. "We are asking for balance. A country cannot be rebuilt while its children die of malnutrition in a hospital named for peace."

As dusk falls over Kabul, the pediatric ward's single generator kicks on for its evening rotation of power. In the dim light, Dr. Hamid moves between patients, doing what she can with what little she has — a daily negotiation between promises made and promises kept.

"We are grateful for what help does come," she said. "But gratitude does not fill an empty medicine cabinet. Somewhere, this money exists. We just need it to arrive here, where the children are waiting."
